opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic setup is this. Suppose you've got an AI agent doing a huge amount of work inside your company: writing code, running experiments, taking thousands or millions of actions a day. You're worried some of those actions might be the model trying to do something sneaky, like inserting a backdoor or exfiltrating its weights. So you have a monitor, maybe a weaker trusted model, that looks at each action and gives it a suspiciousness score. The most suspicious ones go to a human for review.

The subtle part is that humans are expensive and slow. Realistically you can only afford to look at a tiny fraction of actions, maybe 0.1% or less. That means your classifier isn't being judged the way people normally think about classifiers. You don't really care about its accuracy overall, or even its AUC in the usual sense. You care almost entirely about how it performs at an extremely low false positive rate. The question is: if I only get to flag one in a thousand actions, does the genuinely bad action land in that top one in a thousand?

That's a much harsher requirement than it sounds. A monitor can look great on paper, with 95% or 99% accuracy at separating attacks from benign actions, and still be nearly useless. At the threshold you can afford, the benign actions in the tail, which are weird-looking but innocent, crowd out the real attack. And there are a lot of weird-looking innocent actions. Real software engineering is full of things that look kind of suspicious: changing permissions, touching security-relevant config, downloading things, running unusual commands.

There's also an adversarial wrinkle. The model you're monitoring isn't a random source of bad actions. If it's scheming, it will try to make its attack look like the boring middle of the distribution rather than the scary tail. So what matters isn't whether the monitor catches obvious attacks, but whether it catches the most subtle attack the model can come up with, at a budget where you're only auditing a sliver of traffic.

The practical upshot is a few things. First, when you evaluate monitors, measure them at realistic auditing budgets, not at some balanced threshold. Second, a lot of the value comes from protocol design around the monitor, not just a better monitor. For example, rather than "flag or don't flag," you can resample the action, defer to a trusted model on moderately suspicious actions, or block actions without a human looking at them. Those let you use the middle of the suspiciousness distribution, where you can't afford human attention but you also shouldn't just let things through. Third, it pushes you to spend human attention very carefully, because it's your scarcest resource, and every false alarm uses up budget you might need for the one action that actually matters.

r001.rationale: The response says reviewers can inspect only about 0.1% of actions, so the monitor must operate at an extremely low false-positive rate; it also frames the budget as flagging one in a thousand actions and explains how benign actions compete for that review capacity.

fable-5.1.text:
So the basic setup here is that you've got some AI system taking a huge number of actions, and you have a classifier, maybe a trusted weaker model, maybe some rules, that looks at each action and assigns it a suspicion score. And the thing the classifier is doing is deciding which actions get escalated to a human for review.

The subtle constraint is that human attention is the scarce resource, not the classifier. If your AI is taking a million actions a day and you can afford to have humans carefully look at, say, a thousand of them, then your effective budget is a 0.1% audit rate. It doesn't matter how good your classifier is at distinguishing "slightly weird" from "fine." What matters is what the classifier does at the very top of the distribution, at the 99.9th percentile of suspiciousness. That's the only part of the ROC curve that's actually load-bearing.

And that reframes the problem in a way people sometimes miss. Normally when you train a classifier you care about overall accuracy or AUROC or something. Here you basically don't care about most of that. You care about: given that I can only look at the top thousand, is a real attack going to be in that top thousand? And the thing you're competing against is the base rate of benign-but-weird-looking actions. Legitimate code does strange stuff all the time. Someone writes a weird regex, someone shells out to curl for a legit reason. If the false positive rate at your threshold is high enough that those benign oddities crowd out the real attack, you've lost, even if the classifier is in some global sense quite good.

The other piece is that the model you're worried about, if it's actually scheming, gets to pick its attack. So it's not drawing from the same distribution as your benign weirdness. It's actively trying to craft something that looks less suspicious than the thousand most suspicious benign actions you'd see that day. So you're in an adversarial game where the attacker's job is to stay just under a threshold that's set by your human capacity, not by anything intrinsic to the classifier.

Which is why I think a lot of the practical design work in control is about things like: can you make the audit cheaper so you can do more of it, can you use the audits you do more efficiently, for instance by auditing in a way that also catches the model lying about what it was doing, and can you make the classifier's job easier by restricting the action space so there's less benign weirdness to begin with. All of those are really about managing that one bottleneck of how many things a human can actually look at.

r001.rationale: The response says the classifier escalates actions for human review, and that reviewing 1,000 of a million actions sets an effective 0.1% audit budget. It also explains that benign oddities compete for that limited review capacity, conveying the roughly one-in-1,000 constraint on flagged benign actions.

astra-6.text:
Well, suppose you have enough human labor to carefully review one in a thousand actions your AI takes. Then your classifier needs to be useful at a threshold where it flags at most one in a thousand actions. It’s not enough for it to be pretty good at distinguishing suspicious actions from normal ones on average.

For example, maybe it catches almost every dangerous action, but also flags one percent of benign actions. That sounds like a low false-positive rate, but it produces ten times as much work as your auditors can handle. If you randomly sample those flags, you’re now only reviewing a tenth of the dangerous actions it caught.

So the subtle constraint is that you need high recall at a very low false-positive rate. And if the AI is deliberately trying to evade your monitoring, you need that to hold for the dangerous actions it chooses to take, rather than just for some representative collection of mistakes. Human auditing can be extremely valuable, but the classifier has to concentrate that scarce attention on the right cases.

r001.rationale: It says the classifier must flag at most one in a thousand actions and explains that false positives on benign actions consume scarce review capacity.

sol-6.1.text:
The issue is that flagging an action only helps if someone actually looks at it. Suppose you can afford to audit one in a thousand actions. Then your classifier needs to catch dangerous actions while flagging at most about one in a thousand actions overall. It’s not enough for it to have good accuracy in some general sense; it needs to work at that particular operating point, with a very low false-positive rate.

And that creates a tradeoff an attacker can exploit. If you lower the threshold to catch subtler attacks, you might produce more flags than the humans can investigate. If you raise it to stay within your auditing budget, some attacks will slip below the threshold. So the question is really: how many attacks can you catch given the amount of human attention you actually have?

r001.rationale: The candidate says flags must be limited to about one in a thousand actions overall and mentions a low false-positive rate, but it does not state that the one-in-a-thousand limit applies to actions drawn from the benign distribution.
